schools.summary: Gill weighs the absolute 'my eye hath seen all things' — Job an eyewitness to some of God's works and discerning others with enlightened understanding, yet not to be pressed to omniscience, for many things in nature his eye never saw.
Henry hears a man forced, as Paul was by the Corinthians, to commend his own knowledge in self-justification, and warns that disputants are tempted to magnify themselves and vilify their brethren.

Clarke: 'Ye have brought nothing new to me; I know those maxims as well as you'; Wesley refers 'all this' to the power and wisdom of God, known both by seeing (observation) and by hearing from his ancestors.

themes: mine eye hath seen all this

schools.summary: Gill keeps it concrete: Job's knowledge is the same as his friends' concerning God's perfections and his providences, ordinary and extraordinary.

Keil and Delitzsch read the dative as ethical ('made it intelligible to itself') and 'not inferior' as 'he does not stand back behind them,' knowledge equal to theirs (cf. ch. 12:3); Ellicott renders 'I fall not short of you,' and finds the inscrutableness of God driving Job to reason with Him.

outliers.note: Draws from the contest the lesson that truth may be spoken for God by what is not reckoned orthodox, and that 'more ultimate truth may exist in honest doubt than in half the creeds,' quoting Tennyson.

themes: what ye know I know also
the longing to reason with God

schools.summary: Gill reads 'surely' as 'therefore' — Job will have no more to do with his friends as judges but appeal to God, the Judge of all the earth who will do right; not the language of prayer merely.

Clarke fixes the particle as a wish ('O that'), spoken with reference to a court: 'O that God himself would appear!'; Wesley: 'I had rather debate the matter with God than with you,' unafraid to present his cause to a witness of his integrity.

Henry: Job could find no satisfaction talking to his friends and longed to reason with God, who would not be so hard on him — the confidence of those whose hearts do not condemn them of reigning hypocrisy.

themes: I would speak to the Almighty
the boldness of a clear conscience

schools.summary: Gill owns the harshness — Job in passion retorts the friends' charge — but softens 'lies' to falsehoods or untruths, or doctrinal lies like the false prophets' untempered mortar.

Clarke: 'physicians of no value' means feeble reasoners and inefficient healers; every ancient wise man professed the healing art, so the retort is double-edged; 'forgers' (taphal, to sew together) is surgical — 'chirurgeons of falsity.'

Ellicott: Job retorts in terms not more deferential than theirs, calling them patchers-up of falsehood and physicians powerless to heal or understand; Keil and Delitzsch set the line at the head of the strophe (to v.11) and name the fault — advocacy of God that accepts his person.
Gill reads the wish as regret they ever broke the silence of the first seven days, since their speech was neither true nor comforting.

Clarke ties the line to Prov. 17:28 ('even a fool holding his peace is counted wise') as a general apophthegm of all nations, the occasion for his opinion that Job is not ancient and Solomon its likelier author.
Ellicott finds the sentiment 'singularly like' Prov. 17:28: their wisdom will consist in listening to Job's wisdom, not displaying their folly.
Henry: silence would conceal their ignorance and ill-nature, and is not only an evidence of wisdom but a means of it, giving time to think and hear.

outliers.note: Uses the proverb's likeness to Prov. 17:28 to argue that the high antiquity claimed for Job is unfounded, and that Solomon is the likelier author, or the book at least not written till his day.

themes: hold your peace, it is wisdom
silence as wisdom and its means
the date and authorship of Job

schools.summary: Gill marks the reversal Job asks — friends to be hearers not speakers — insisting that, afflicted as he was, his reason and wisdom were not driven out but ready for his own defence, even before God.
Clarke fixes the forensic setting: the speeches are conceived as delivered in a court, the terms ('reasoning,' 'pleadings') being those of counsellors pleading against one another.
Henry reads it as a claim of justice — hear, and not merely hear but hearken — for many a man, could he be fairly heard, would be fairly acquitted even by those who run him down.

themes: reason not driven out by affliction

schools.summary: Gill unfolds the double fault — pleading God's justice by denying he afflicts good men, yet speaking wickedly of Job as a hypocrite — needlessly, since they could uphold that justice and yet allow God afflicts the good.
Clarke: to support their own cause they assert God could not so afflict Job without flagrant iniquity, and so 'tell lies for God's sake, and wickedly contend for their Maker.'
Ellicott hears a sublime truth: God, no respecter of persons, desires no favour shown to Himself; to flatter Him damages their cause, for words as well as actions are weighed by a God of truth.
Henry: God needs no such advocates and can plead for himself; a good intention will not sanctify a bad word — 'pious frauds are impious cheats.'

themes: God is a God of truth

schools.summary: Gill draws the courtroom sense: to accept persons is what judges must never do; the friends considered only what God was, but neglected Job's cause, giving it against him because he was poor and miserable.
Keil and Delitzsch name the offence: the friends set themselves up as God's advocates and 'accept his person,' as one accepts a gratifying gift, a partiality God will not leave unpunished.
Clarke asks whether they think to conciliate God's esteem by telling lies in his favour; Wesley glosses 'accept his person' as judging by the person, not the right of the cause.
Henry: God's cause is so just it needs no such methods; he can plead for himself (Judg. 6:31), and to condemn a man their consciences might acquit makes his cause suffer by their management.

Gill takes the searching judicially — 'first in his own cause seemeth just, but his neighbour searcheth him' (Prov. 18:17): the friends seem right in their own eyes, but God the searcher of hearts shows the fallacy of their arguments.
Clarke turns the question on their conscience: were they tried as Job is, how would they appear? and warns against thinking to deceive God as an undiscerning mortal.
Ellicott glosses the mockery precisely: 'as one man, with mingled flattery and deception, seeks to impose upon another.'
Henry weighs it as a summons to self-examination: it is good to the upright that God search him ('Search me, O God'), but bad to the man who looks one way and rows another; God is not mocked.

themes: is it good that he search you out

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the doubled Hebrew ('in reproving he will reprove you'): God never leaves sin unreproved, rebuking by Spirit, word, ministers, and afflictive providences, in love or in hot displeasure.
Clarke keeps the warning heavy: they may expect not only God's disapprobation but his hot displeasure.
Henry: if they accept persons even secretly, God will resent it as a great provocation, as a prince would a base act done under his name; what we do amiss we shall certainly be reproved for.

themes: reproof by Spirit, word, and providence

schools.summary: Gill unfolds the 'excellency' — in God's name, nature, and works — and the alternative renderings 'his height' (the Most High) and 'his lifting up' upon a throne of judgment (Targum).
Clarke: the very apprehension of God's wrath is sufficient to crush them to nothing.
Henry hears Job speak as one who himself feared God: there is in God a dreadful excellency, his very goodness dreadful to sinful man, and a holy awe of it should make us afraid to offend (Neh. 5:9).

themes: the Most High on his throne

schools.summary: Gill ranges the senses of 'remembrances' — the friends' arguments and memorable sentences, or the memorials (houses, wealth, learning) by which men hope to outlive themselves — all but ashes; men are dust and ashes (Aben Ezra).

Clarke: 'your memorable sayings are proverbs of dust,' the second clause 'swelling heaps of mire,' high-flown speeches all sound and no sense; Wesley: mementos like ashes, our mortality a reason to fear offending God.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'proverbs of dust... strongholds of clay'; Ellicott gives both parallelisms — saws worthless as dust, or 'your high fabrics are fabrics of clay.'
Henry: our meanness and mortality should make us fear God and not trample our brethren; records Bishop Patrick's turn — the friends' remonstrances 'no better than dust... heaps of dirt.'

debates.question: Do the 'remembrances' name the friends' memorable sayings, or their own frail bodies and strongholds?

sides.position: their memorable sayings and arguments, proverbs of dust
the second line taken independently, 'your strongholds/high fabrics are of clay'

schools.summary: Gill catches the occasion: Job saw his friends about to interrupt and desired them silent that he might go on.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'be silent from me' — he alone will defend the cause they abandoned, let happen what may ('quidquid est'); Ellicott hears him bracing for a declaration like chapter 19, resolved to face God in judgment.
Clarke: 'your pleadings are irrelevant; it is high time you had done. I will now defend myself and leave the cause to its issue.'
Henry opens the long meditation to the speech's end: Job takes fast hold of his integrity, welcoming every event — 'come what will, with a heart well prepared he is ready for it.'

themes: let me alone that I may speak
let come on me what will

schools.summary: Gill reads 'take my flesh in my teeth' as biting the lips to keep in his words: 'I will not do it.'

Keil and Delitzsch: a proverbial phrase found nowhere else — intent on life as a beast on its prey — with 'life in one's hand' the standing idiom for extreme danger (Judg. 12:3; 1 Sam. 19:5); Ellicott would drop the question and read a bold resolve, 'at all risks I will take my flesh in my teeth.'

Clarke: a proverb of daring — 'I risk everything, I run all hazards, fearless of consequences' (1 Sam. 28:21); Wesley makes it the reason for craving speech — he must tear himself to pieces if he had no vent for grief.

debates.question: Is the verse a wondering question or a bold resolve?

sides.position: a question — why should I thus imperil myself by speaking?
not interrogative but a defiant resolve — 'come what may, I will take my flesh in my teeth'

schools.summary: Gill lays bare the double reading — Keri 'in him' (which the AV follows), Ketib 'not' ('I shall not hope') — and allows the second agrees with Job's other professions of no hope of long life.

Keil and Delitzsch note it is one of eighteen Ketib-'lo'/Keri-'lo' passages (Job 6:21 another), their own rendering keeping the trust; Ellicott presses the Ketib — 'Behold he will slay me, I have no hope; yet will I maintain my ways' — judging the familiar trust-rendering 'very doubtful.'

Clarke weighs the manuscripts — 29 of Kennicott and De Rossi, plus Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, Chaldee — for 'him,' concluding 'our translators followed the best reading'; the trust is faith's summit, 'I shall come forth as gold.'
Henry keeps the received reading as a high expression of faith — to trust God though he slay us, well pleased with him as friend even when he seems an enemy.

debates.question: Does the disputed word (Ketib lo / Keri lo) yield 'yet will I trust in him' or 'I have no hope'?

sides.position: 'yet will I trust in him' (Keri, the pronoun) — the received, best-attested reading
'I have no hope' (Ketib, the negative) — the better and likelier reading

themes: though he slay me yet will I trust
I will maintain mine own ways

schools.summary: Gill: Job rests not on his works but on the Lord himself for a spiritual and eternal salvation, knowing God as his Saviour and living Redeemer.
Clarke reads the second clause as the proof of sincerity: a wicked man could not stand before God, and were Job a secret sinner he would not dare make this appeal.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the forensic frame — the confession and declaration Job longs to lay before God; Ellicott makes the verse the hinge of the book, Job (outside the pale of Israel) sharing the faith of God's people and trusting God unreservedly, as Abraham did (Gen. 15:6).

outliers.note: Argues that Job, probably living outside the pale of Israel, uniquely shared the faith of God's chosen people, trusting God as the sinner's hope while his friends rested on vague generalities — exhibiting in Job what was manifest in Abraham.

themes: a hypocrite shall not come before him
trust as the mark of sincerity
the faith of Abraham in Job

schools.summary: Gill reads 'in hearing hear' as a plea that the friends not merely attend but keep attending and hear him out, lest they rise or interrupt as he speaks so boldly.
Wesley marks the structure: Job now 'comes more closely to his business, the foregoing verses being mostly by way of preface.'
Keil and Delitzsch render 'hear, O hear my confession, and let my declaration echo in your ears,' the 'declaration' a rare word found in the Hebrew OT only in Job — the formal opening of a defence.

themes: the formal opening of the defence

schools.summary: Gill unfolds the legal image: Job had reviewed and arranged his cause in regular form, and could draw the confident conclusion.
Clarke: 'I am ready to come into court, and care not how many I contend with, provided they speak truth'; Wesley: 'I have seriously considered my case, and am ready to plead.'
Keil and Delitzsch render 'I have arranged the cause; I know that I shall maintain the right,' carrying it into the challenge 'who then can contend with me?'

Henry grounds the certainty in Job's knowing his Redeemer lived (ch. 19:25): the upright, through Christ, face no condemnation — yet not a claim to justify every word, only that his cause in the main is good.

themes: I know I shall be justified
the peace of a settled conscience

schools.summary: Gill hears a man daring any comer to the lists, and reads the words also of Christ the surety justified as a public person, and of the believer acquitted of every charge; Job would rather God himself plead with him.
Clarke: 'Let my accuser come forward; I will defend my cause' — defending himself will be as respiration, or he will be so silent as scarcely to breathe while his adversary speaks.
Ellicott calls it a marvellous confession: to hold his tongue is to give up faith in his salvation and his innocence, and so to perish — 'to give up my innocence is to give up Him in whom I live.'
Henry: if he holds his tongue and does not speak for himself, his silence will for ever silence him, for he shall give up the ghost; if not cleared, let him be eased.

themes: if I hold my tongue I shall give up the ghost

schools.summary: Gill marks that this is spoken to God himself, not Zophar in God's place: before pleadings begin Job would settle the terms, asking two things.
Clarke names the two — withdraw the afflicting hand, and let not the dread terrify — with the reasons: no man can plead under bodily torment or the overwhelming majesty of the judge.

Keil and Delitzsch tie it to the two conditions of ch. 9:34 (respite and no overwhelming majesty); Ellicott glosses 'I will not hide myself' as 'I shall not be hidden,' a different word from Adam's hiding in Gen. 3:10.

themes: a fair field not a favour

schools.summary: Gill reads the first condition as a plea against pain: unless God's afflicting hand be removed, Job cannot command his reasoning, for bodily affliction affects soul, memory, understanding, and judgment.
Wesley joins both petitions: 'suspend my torments during my pleading, that my mind may be at liberty; present not thyself in terrible majesty, nor deal in rigorous justice.'

Ellicott: 'cease to torture me bodily and terrify me mentally'; Keil and Delitzsch note the word, though usually the open palm, means here the heavy hand of God whose pressure would prevent Job's answering.

themes: let not thy dread make me afraid
the rod and the terror laid by

schools.summary: Gill sets the alternatives as a courtroom: God may call and Job answer, or Job speak and God answer — either way he is ready, asking only fair pleadings.
Keil and Delitzsch render the verse the same way, as the last of the terms following the two petitions — God to grant relief, then open the cause by questioning or hearing.
Wesley alone warns that the proposal 'savoured of self-confidence and of irreverence towards God,' for which Job is later reproved (ch. 38:2-3).

Henry holds boldness and limit together: Job doubted not the goodness of his cause, yet how hard to reason with God on a bed of pain — a folly to put off repentance to a death-bed; still the upright may come boldly to the throne of grace.

debates.question: Is Job's offer to plead a fitting boldness or an over-confidence God will rebuke?

sides.position: a reverent, upright boldness that finds mercy at the throne of grace
a self-confidence and irreverence for which God later reproves him

outliers.note: Judges the whole proposal to savour of self-confidence and irreverence towards God, the sort of speech for which the Lord afterwards reproves Job out of the whirlwind (ch. 38-40).

themes: call thou and I will answer
access to the throne of grace

schools.summary: Gill: the heap of words means all sorts of sins, Job asking their quality and quantity; yet records Schultens's turn that the interrogation has the force of a negation ('how few') — Job's sins few beside his affliction.

Clarke demands the bill of particulars: 'to say I must be a sinner to be afflicted is nothing; tell me the sins, show me the proofs'; Wesley: 'that I am a sinner I confess, but not guilty of such crimes as my friends suppose; if so, do thou discover it.'
Ellicott holds both sides together — Job's claim to righteousness runs beside a deep confession of sin, understood only in the light of Him who convicts of sin before convincing of righteousness.

Henry takes it three ways — passionate complaint, prudent appeal from the friends' censures, or pious request like Elihu's 'teach thou me' (ch. 34:32) — a true penitent willing to know the worst of himself.

themes: make me to know my transgression
confession beside the claim of innocence
the appeal past the friends to God

schools.summary: Gill sets aside the lighter senses and reads a withdrawal of God's face and favour — once enjoyed, now hidden — the Lord's end being to try Job's patience and integrity, sin not always the cause.

Keil and Delitzsch hear a conscience unable to square the affliction with God's justice: Job, who prayed 'remember not the sins of my youth' (Ps. 25:7), can only take his suffering as their entailed inheritance.
Clarke: 'Why do I no longer enjoy thy approbation? Treatest me as if I were the vilest of sinners?'

Henry: this, not the outward losses, is the sorest trouble — favours suspended, terrors inflicted, God holding him for an enemy (ch. 6:4); Job's sufferings typical of Christ's, from whom God hid his face (Isa. 53:3).
Gill draws the image — a withered leaf driven by the wind — of Job's outward frailty, not his spiritual estate (a good man's leaf withers not); to break so weak a thing adds affliction to affliction.
Clarke sharpens it to God's dignity: 'Is it becoming thy dignity to concern thyself with a creature so contemptible?'
Ellicott hears a confession bordering on despair, Job's driven leaf and stubble approaching the psalmist's picture of the ungodly, chaff before the wind (Ps. 1:4).
Henry reads a pleading of utter inability — 'is it for thy honour to trample one already down?' — turned to hope, for God will not break the bruised reed (Matt. 12:20).
Gill will not let 'bitter things' be sins recorded (Job is asking to be told his sins), but afflictions — bitter, grievous, not joyous — that God writes against him.

Clarke: 'the indictment is filled with bitter charges'; the levities of youth he owns, but no ground for charges against an unimpeachable life; Wesley glosses 'writest' as 'appointest or inflictest,' a metaphor from judges who wrote their sentences.

Ellicott calls the confession 'exquisitely plaintive and affecting'; Keil and Delitzsch feel the perplexity — Job can only take the affliction as the inheritance of youthful sins, having none of his mature years to reproach.

Henry: God writes bitter things against his best servants to humble and prove them; the sins of youth are the smart of age (Jer. 31:18-19), time not wearing out sin's guilt — the design, to make us possess and so forsake our iniquities.

debates.question: Are the 'bitter things' God writes sins recorded, or afflictions inflicted?

sides.position: afflictions, bitter and grievous, written against him
the charges of an indictment / sentence inflicted

themes: time wears not out sin's guilt

schools.summary: Gill takes the stocks as a punishment and reservation for further affliction, hemming Job in; notes Aben Ezra's 'feet in lime' (steps marked) but thinks it foreign to Job's mind.

Clarke fills in the picture — the clog tied to slaves' feet, still used in the West Indies as 'the pudding' — and reads 'lookest narrowly' and the 'print upon the heels' of God seeing every step, or pursuing him as a hound by the scent.

Ellicott confesses a real difficulty in the pronouns (illustrated by Ps. 88:8; 142:7), the subject being the fetter, or Job, or man of the next chapter; the word for fetter (only here and Job 33:11) may be feminine; Keil and Delitzsch keep the same watching-and-wasting sense.

outliers.note: Notes a genuine grammatical difficulty in the pronouns of vv.27-28 (feminine and second-masculine future being alike), the subject variously the fetter, Job himself, or man — probably the object of all this watching and persecution.

schools.summary: Gill ties the verse to the driven leaf of v.25 and reads it of Job's own frail body, like a rotten tree (Ben Melech), consuming and clothed with worms and clods of dust.

Clarke: 'I am like a vessel of skin, rotten with age, or a garment corroded by the moth' (so the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic); Wesley marks the third person — 'this poor frail creature, this body of mine,' perhaps pointed at with his finger, consumes and pines away.
Henry allows both subjects — man consuming like a moth-eaten garment, or God consuming Job like rottenness and moth (Hos. 5:12) — for man at his best wears fast, and soonest under God's rebukes.
